text: I’m a returning student kicking off this Data Structures course in my first semester, trying to juggle it with another heavy class, and I’m left with mixed impressions. The conceptual explanations are solid enough to ground the ideas, but the real-world examples feel thin, like we’re told what a binary search tree is without seeing how it actually behaves in a chunk of code I’ve tweaked myself. I kept up with nearly every lecture, and I’ve been to office hours once where a TA walked me through a bug I couldn’t shake on a small project, but I still walked away wondering how the assessments are supposed to map to what we’re told in lectures. The collaboration expectations feel murky; peers help each other more than staff does, and I’m not sure what count as a good group contribution for the weekly tasks. The mix of quizzes and a couple of bigger problem sets doesn’t line up with the lecture pace, and I’m left second-guessing whether I’m studying the right patterns for the exams. Overall, it’s not a total mess, but that mismatch sticks out, and I’m still rusty in spots I’d hoped would be clearer by now.

I’m new to the discipline and took Machine Learning mostly out of curiosity, and I’ll admit the course felt useful but not enjoyable. The explanations were solid on concepts, but the real-world examples never felt fleshed out enough to connect to what I’m seeing in labs or projects, so I spent most of the weeks relying on recordings and my own notes to pretend I understood how the pieces fit. The structure assumed more prior knowledge than I expected, and I kept thinking, “wait, do we really need that upstairs theorem for the homework?” The grading felt thorough in its comments, but the feedback arrived late enough that it didn’t help much for the next assignment, which was frustrating when time was ticking. I mostly worked alone, with a few small discussion threads that went nowhere; collaboration never clicked for me. My turning point came late in the semester during the final exam prep when I realized I could explain the high-level idea to a friend but couldn’t reproduce a concrete workflow for tuning a model without stumbling, which left me with a disappointing sense of what I actually learned. Overall, it’s a course I can see the value in, even if I didn’t enjoy it.

I started off really engaged in Calculus II with Prof. Alvarez, and the organization of lectures and problem sets was solid, which helped since the LMS and submission flow are smooth. But the deadlines stacked up unexpectedly, so pacing felt rough and I found myself scrambling between topics, especially around the more advanced integrals. Still, the course fills prerequisite gaps better than I expected, and classmates often helped each other more than staff did, which kept us moving when I was uncertain about a concept like improper integrals.

I’m a returning student juggling a couple of demanding courses, and Operating Systems felt like it was testing my rusty basics more than anything else. Prof. Rios is clear in lectures, but the grading and the platform quirks created avoidable stress, especially when deadlines piled up and emails to support didn’t get quick answers. The course leaned heavy on reports and long writeups, not just quick problem sets, so I had to map out a week-by-week plan around the big deliverables. It helps that the class works better if you’ve got a study group; I leaned on a TA during office hours for one on one caveats about the project week, and I still remember a memorably tense second midterm week where the format felt like a surprise. Overall, it’s not a breeze, but the teaching style and the exam feel were fair enough.

Took Computer Networks with Prof. Cohen while working full-time, and my main takeaway is how the lectures feel solid on concepts but the concrete stuff never sticks—like the examples barely scratch the surface, so I left thinking, “okay, I get the why, not the how.” The assessments felt mismatched: quick-score quizzes peppered with code-reading questions, but the explanations behind the answers were thin, and the fast feedback rarely clarified where I went wrong, which didn’t help when deadlines piled up. I did appreciate the late-semester turning point around a networking lab, but the support channel, especially email, dragged when I needed guidance fast. Compared to the other course I took that term, this one left me tired and resigned rather than confident about applying anything to a real project.

Honestly, Cyber Security Basics was a mixed ride: I started off engaged, but my attendance faded as the semester dragged on and the workload piled up. I’m comfortable with proofs, not so much with system work, so the material felt a better fit once I leaned on the TAs and the forums to translate concepts into something usable. The project-heavy rhythm and high-stakes exams kept me honest, and the grading comments were thorough but came a bit late, which didn’t help when I was chasing feedback before a midterm. Office hours were a lifesaver, especially when I needed a quick sanity check on a threat model, and the instructor was solid, even if I didn’t always love the pace or the late rubric tweaks. Overall, it’s okay, and it helped for industry talk, but the practical parts pressed hard against my comfort zone.

I took Database Systems hoping it’d feel practical for industry work, but I left with mixed feelings and a rough mid-semester crunch that threw off my momentum. Dr. Chen is solid in lectures, yet the prerequisite feel like more than what was promised, and I found myself relying mostly on recordings and notes rather than live class energy. The LMS and submission flow are smooth, which helped during a tense week, but the assessments—a mix that didn’t line up well with what got covered in lectures—made it hard to feel confident about what mattered. I’d only recommend taking it if you’re prepared to put in extra prep and tolerate a bit of sloppy communication on administrative bits, plus don’t expect a tidy payoff.
